food.text: Ethiopia lies within the native range of Coffea arabica, which grows naturally in the highlands of southern Ethiopia, South Sudan and northern Kenya. In the 2024/25 marketing year the country exported about 7.43 million bags of coffee, earning around US$2.89 billion. Roughly 5.9 million farmers are directly engaged in coffee production.

The famine of 1983 to 1985 was the worst to hit Ethiopia in a century. It affected 7.75 million people and left approximately 300,000 to 1.2 million dead. About 2.5 million people were internally displaced, and almost 200,000 children were orphaned.
The extreme climate variability of East Africa makes the region vulnerable to cycles of drought and flood. In the 20th century this led to food insecurity and climate migration.

From 1974 to 1991, Ethiopia was ruled by a Marxist dictatorship. Coffee farms were consolidated into large collective farms and required to sell to the government at a subsidized price. After 1991, the government allowed farms to form cooperatives and set fair prices.

Harar coffee comes from the Eastern highlands of Ethiopia and is known for a distinctive fruity, wine flavour. It is dry processed, with sorting and processing done almost entirely by hand. The shells of the coffee bean are used in a tea called hasher-qahwa.

In 2008 the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange was established to modernize the trade of agricultural commodities including coffee. At first, coffee was pooled by grade and region, so international buyers could not identify the washing station, cooperative or producer behind a lot. Specialty roasters and importers criticized this for diluting the premium value of Ethiopia's most distinctive regional coffees.

On 26 October 2006, Oxfam accused Starbucks of asking the National Coffee Association to block a US trademark application from Ethiopia for three coffee beans: Sidamo, Harar and Yirgacheffe. Oxfam claimed this could deny Ethiopian coffee farmers potential annual earnings of up to £47m.

According to Human Rights Watch, more than half of the mortality in the 1983 to 1985 Ethiopian famine could be attributed to human rights abuses that caused the famine to come earlier, strike harder and extend further. Human Rights Watch and Oxfam said the famine was in part created by the government's military policies: counter-insurgency strategies against Tigray People's Liberation Front guerrilla-soldiers, and "social transformation" in non-insurgent areas. The article says the Derg restricted food supplies as part of this strategy and deliberately multiplied the famine's effects, and that around 1.2 million people died. In fall 1984 the hardest hit regions were Tigray, Wollo and Eritrea, which had extremely limited road networks and were the scenes of longstanding anti-government rebellions.

The 1982 harvest in Ethiopia was the largest ever, except in central and eastern Tigray. The 1983 main harvest was the third largest on record, yet famine still recurred in Tigray. In May 1984 the government's relief commission claimed that failure of the short belg rains was a catastrophic drought, though belg crops give none of the yield in most of Tigray. The article says the commission portrayed the famine as solely the result of drought and overpopulation and tried to deny the armed conflict in the famine-affected regions, while the Derg restricted food supplies as military policy against Tigray.

In Kenya, the Somali ostrich is farmed for meat, feathers and eggs. In Somalia, a 2006 report to the IUCN said the bird had been common in the central and southern regions in the 1970s and 1980s. Since the country's political disintegration and the lack of any effective wildlife conservation, uncontrolled hunting for meat, medicinal products and eggs has shrunk its range and numbers there, and the bird faces eradication in the Horn of Africa.

art.text: Ethiopian art is heavily influenced by the country's long-standing Christian tradition. That makes it different from most African art, where traditional African religion was dominant until the 20th century.

The rock-cut monolithic churches of Lalibela, in Ethiopia's Amhara Region, were declared a World Heritage Site in 1978. To some Christians the town is one of Ethiopia's holiest cities and a center of pilgrimage.

The Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science was inaugurated in Addis Ababa on 4 October 2022 by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Its 9-metre circular exhibition building is dubbed the "ring of wisdom" to denote human ability and skillfulness to create objects.
art.source_title: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science
tags: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

art.text: Apart from Islamic manuscripts, paper only came into general use in Ethiopia in the twentieth century. Before that, parchment (berānnā) was used, and most Ethiopian manuscripts are written in Ge'ez, the ancient liturgical language of Ethiopia.

The museum in Addis Ababa also holds the Dome Theatre, a 450 m2 three-dimensional cinema that is 24 metres high. It can accommodate up to 200 people at once, and its inauguration coincided with the Pan-African Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2022.
art.source_title: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science
tags: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

art.text: Roger Wenman Cowley spent 15 years in Ethiopia as an Anglican missionary and teacher. He commissioned paper copies of Biblical commentaries in Amharic, executed during 1967 to 1977, and 39 of his manuscripts later came to the British Library.

The Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science is part of the Chinese aided Addis Ababa Riverside Development Project Phase II. It lies on 6.78 hectares, and its construction cost 1.1 billion birr, or $21.1 million.
art.source_title: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

war.text: On 3 October 1935, two hundred thousand soldiers of Italy's Royal Army attacked Ethiopia from Eritrea without any prior declaration of war. The Second Italo-Ethiopian War, called a war of aggression, is regarded as the largest colonial campaign in history. It lasted until May 1936, and Italy dropped between 300 and 500 tons of mustard gas on military and civilian targets, violating the 1925 Geneva Protocol. By all estimates hundreds of thousands of Ethiopian civilians died, and some historians describe the invasion as genocide.

The Eritrean-Ethiopian War, also called the Badme War, ran from May 6, 1998 to June 18, 2000. Over 500,000 troops fought on both sides, making it the biggest war in the world at the time. It reportedly killed between 70,000 and 300,000 people combined, and displaced a further 600,000. Most international reports put the death toll at around 70,000, while other news reports say "tens of thousands" or "as many as 100,000"; all these figures are contested.

In 1977 Somalia invaded the Ogaden region to back the Western Somali Liberation Front. Ethiopia was saved from defeat by a $1 billion airlift of military supplies, more than 12,000 Cuban soldiers and airmen, and 1,500 Soviet advisors. The Soviet Union had switched sides, withdrawing its support from Somalia.

On 12 September 1974 the Derg, a committee of low-ranking officers and enlisted men, overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in a coup and later made Ethiopia a Marxist-Leninist state. On 27 August 1975 Haile Selassie was killed by Ethiopian military officers in the National Palace in Addis Ababa, while his daughter Princess Ijigayehu, his sister Princess Tenagnework and many of his relatives were detained. The civil war that followed, against many rebel groups, lasted until 28 May 1991 and left at least 1.4 million people dead, about 1 million of them related to famine and the rest from combat and other violence.

During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, Haile Selassie made a pilgrimage to the churches at Lalibela, at considerable risk of capture. He then returned to his capital in April 1936, and Italian forces captured the town shortly after.

When the Italians launched their 1935 invasion, they seized Aksum on 15 October. Its famous obelisk was torn from its site and sent to Rome, to be placed symbolically in front of the Ministry of Colonies. Adwa had been taken on 6 October, a symbolic place because of Italy's earlier defeat there.

The Derg launched the Qey Shibir, or Red Terror, in 1976 as a campaign of violent political repression, mainly against the EPRP and later MEISON, and escalated it on 3 February 1977 after Mengistu Haile Mariam became Chairman of the Derg. Brutal tactics were used on all sides in the urban guerrilla warfare, including summary executions, assassinations, torture and imprisonment without trial. Its estimated 30,000 to 750,000 victims are believed to be mostly innocents, and many civilians are still missing, thought to have been systematically killed by the Derg. The violence and collateral damage shocked many Ethiopians into supporting rebel groups.

The Ethiopian-Cuban force at Harar and Jijiga, equipped with 300 tanks, 156 artillery pieces and 46 combat aircraft, began pushing the Somalis out of the Ogaden. On 23 January 1978, Cuban armored brigades inflicted the worst losses the Somali forces had taken in a single action since the war began, with Somali casualties possibly as high as 3,000 in the failed attack on Harar. By the end of the war, almost a third of the regular SNA soldiers, three-eighths of the armored units and half of the Somali Air Force had been lost. Ethiopia declared the last border post regained on 23 March 1978.

After Italy's defeat in 1941, nearly 7,000 Italian soldiers took part in a guerrilla war in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia. They hoped the German-Italian army would win in Egypt and let them recapture the territories. The campaign lasted from summer 1941 to autumn 1943.

From 1961 until 1991, Eritrea fought a 30-year war of independence against Ethiopia. During the same period, the Tigray People's Liberation Front allied itself with the Eritrean People's Liberation Front against their common enemy, the Derg. Ironically, the TPLF-led government later ended up at war with Eritrea.

In 1963 the Ogaden Liberation Front, known as 'Nasrallah', began a guerrilla war for self-determination with 300 men, which soon swelled to 3,000. Ethiopia's imperial army responded with a large counterinsurgency campaign, including large-scale artillery bombardments of Somali cities in the Ogaden. An Ethiopian Imperial Army division based at Harar torched Somali villages and carried out mass killings of livestock, and aircraft machine-gunned watering holes to deny the nomadic Somalis water. Thousands of residents were driven out of the Ogaden into Somalia as refugees, and the reprisals helped lead to the first interstate war between Ethiopia and Somalia in 1964.

literature.text: Yemodish Bekele, born in Addis Ababa in 1960, published thirteen books, including poetry, short stories and a novella. She was the first Ethiopian woman to publish her own collection of short stories.

In 1973 and 1974, Emperor Haile Selassie published his autobiography My Life and Ethiopia's Progress. In 1976 it was translated from Amharic into English and annotated by Edward Ullendorff for Oxford University Press.
Since the early 1970s, the Academy of Somali Studies has held award-winning poetry competitions. They were inspired by the traditional poetry competitions held annually throughout Somalia.

In 1979, at the age of 19, Yemodish Bekele won a competition sponsored by the Ministry of Culture and Sports. Twelve of her poems were published in an illustrated collection called 'Abyotawi Gitmoch' ('Revolutionary Poems'). One poem, 'ke maget eske ketema', was about the struggle of women.

Hanna Rubinkowska maintains that Haile Selassie actively practiced "historiographic manipulation". She says he concealed historical materials that seemed to contradict dynastic propaganda and official history.

Yemodish Bekele grew up as the only child of a police officer, reading police newspapers and publications. She later worked for twenty-six years at Polis Ena Ermijaw, the Federal Police newspaper, rising from intern to become its first woman head editor.

Haile Selassie moved certain chronicles into his private library, away from public view. One was aleqa Gabra Igziabiher Elyas' biographical chronicle of the reigns of Lij Iyasu and Empress Zewditu. Rudolf K. Molvaer edited, translated and republished it in 1994.

In 1975 the historian Zewde Gebre-Sellassie published a biography of Emperor Yohannes II. He was distantly related to the emperor, and the book is one of several modern biographies of Ethiopian emperors.

The Somali Studies Association gives the Musa Galaal award to scholars whose work stands out. It is named after the Somali polymath Musa Haji Ismail Galal (1914–1980). In 1994, Charles L. Geshekter, whose mother was Galaal's friend, created an endowment for the prize.
Yaltenabebu Liboch ('Unread Hearts') is a collection of short stories by nine women authors. Population Media Center published the winning selections from a competition among 42 women authors.

Azurit ('Turbulence') is a collection of true stories by several authors who won a competition sponsored by the Population Media Center in 2012, one of several such anthologies among Yemodish Bekele's thirteen books.

science.text: The Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science is a 15,000 m2 science museum in Addis Ababa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed inaugurated it on 4 October 2022. It contains a science and technology exhibition hall dedicated to scientific and developmental research.
science.source_title: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science
tags: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

science.text: Modern higher education in Ethiopia began under Emperor Haile Selassie with the University College of Addis Ababa in 1950. It is now called Addis Ababa University. Haramaya University and the Ambo school of agriculture, today's Ambo University, followed.

The Science and Technology Information Center provides information to support scientific and technological activities in Ethiopia. It was established on 15 December 2011 by a Council of Ministers regulation. In August 2014 it published its first Science and Technology Indicators Report.

The museum's exhibition area is a 9-metre high circular building dubbed the 'ring of wisdom', denoting humanity's endless ability and capacity to continuously create. It stands on 6.78 hectares. Inside, interactive display screens show local solutions in healthcare, finance, cybersecurity and robotics.
science.source_title: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science
tags: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

science.text: The original University College of Addis Ababa was modelled on European-style facilities. Its Arts, Sciences and Education structure included thirteen departments, six of them in Science: Chemistry, Physics, Mathematics, Geography, Biology and Pharmacy.

Ethiopia carried out its first national survey of research and development in 2009, run by the Ministry of Science and Technology. In 2013 the Science and Technology Information Center was mandated to conduct the survey, and it carried out the second one in 2014.
The museum's second portion is the Dome Theatre, a 450 m2 three-dimensional cinema. It is 24 metres high and can hold up to 200 people at once.
science.source_title: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science
tags: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

science.text: Graduate-level training in Ethiopia began at Addis Ababa University in 1979, followed by Alemaya University in 1984. Wondo Genet College of Forestry later trained undergraduates through forestry programs. Jimma, Hawassa and Mekelle University later continued with graduate students.

The Ministry of Science and Higher Education was established in October 2018 by proclamation number 1097/2018. It led development of science, higher education and technical and vocational training. Hirut Woldemariam led it from its foundation to August 2020, and it merged into the Ministry of Education in October 2021.
science.source_title: Ministry of Science and Higher Education (Ethiopia)
tags: Ministry of Science and Higher Education

science.text: The museum's inauguration coincided with the Pan-African Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2022. Abiy Ahmed cited Ethiopia's Digital Economy Strategy and stressed the need for an Artificial Intelligence Institute as part of the country's digital transformation.

tags: Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science

science.text: Ethiopia's science and technology information effort dates to 1977, when the Ethiopian Science and Technology Commission planned a National Scientific and Technological Information and Documentation Center. It was designed as an apex body to coordinate the collection, organization and dissemination of scientific and technological information.
tags: National Scientific and Technological Information and Documentation Center

politics.text: In 1974, amid popular uprisings, the Derg, a military junta, overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie. The uprisings followed a famine that killed an estimated 40,000 to 80,000 Ethiopians between 1972 and 1974, and riots in February 1974 that left five dead. The 82-year-old Selassie was deposed on 12 September and spent his last months under house arrest. With support from the Soviet Union, the Derg began governing Ethiopia as a Marxist–Leninist state, and on 23 November it executed 60 former high officials by firing squad, including his grandson Iskinder Desta, in the killings known as "Black Saturday". The coup ended the Ethiopian Empire and the Solomonic dynasty founded in 1270.

Italy attacked Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 without a prior declaration of war, sending two hundred thousand soldiers from Italian Eritrea. The Second Italo-Ethiopian War was a war of aggression that lasted until May 1936 and is regarded as the largest colonial campaign in history. Italian aircraft dropped 330 tons of mustard gas in violation of the 1925 Geneva Protocol, and Italian troops used it in aerial bombardments against combatants and civilians. By all estimates hundreds of thousands of Ethiopian civilians died as a result of the invasion, which some historians have described as genocide.

The Ethiopian Civil War was fought between the Derg and Ethiopian-Eritrean rebels from 12 September 1974 to 28 May 1991. Groups such as the Eritrean Peoples Liberation Front, the Tigrayan Peoples Liberation Front and the Oromo Liberation Front resisted the Soviet-backed junta. The Derg used the Qey Shibir, or Red Terror, to repress them, a campaign of violent political repression in which summary executions, assassinations, torture and imprisonment without trial were used. The war left at least 1.4 million people dead, 1 million of them linked to famine and the rest killed in combat and other violence.

In November 2020, Ethiopia began a military offensive in Tigray in response to attacks on army units stationed there, starting the Tigray war. The dispute followed the Tigray Region's TPLF holding elections on 9 September 2020 despite the federal government's cancellation. By March 2022, as many as 500,000 people had died from violence and famine.

In June 1916, rumors spread that the uncrowned Emperor Lij Iyasu had converted to Islam under Ottoman influence, and he was charged with apostasy. Ras Tafari Mekonnen, later Emperor Haile Selassie, deposed him in a coup on September 26, 1916. The Allies claimed he had converted, though there was no concrete evidence.

Haile Selassie introduced Ethiopia's 1931 constitution and abolished slavery in 1942. In 1963 he presided over the formation of the Organisation of African Unity, the precursor of the African Union, and served as its first chairman.

Haile Selassie dissolved the Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea, which the United Nations General Assembly had established in 1950. He annexed Eritrea as one of Ethiopia's provinces and fought to prevent Eritrean secession. In 1961 the Eritrean War for Independence began and lasted 30 years; first Selassie, then the Soviet-backed junta that succeeded him, tried to hold Eritrea by force, and the Imperial Army carried out multiple atrocities against Eritrean separatists in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

In 1977 Somalia invaded to back the Western Somali Liberation Front in the Ogaden, delivering a major blow to the Derg. This triggered a large-scale Soviet and Cuban military intervention that drove back Somali forces.

In 1916 Ethiopia's uncrowned Emperor, Lij Iyasu, was alleged to have converted to Islam under Ottoman influence. Ras Tafari Mekonnen, later Emperor Haile Selassie, carried out a coup on 26 September 1916, supported by the Allied Powers. There was no concrete evidence of any conversion.

Ketema Yifru, a former Ethiopian foreign minister, was arrested without charges by the Derg, the military regime that imprisoned many former ministers after the fall of Emperor Haile Selassie. He spent eight years in prison under harsh conditions and was released in 1982, with no charges ever formally filed. He then joined the United Nations World Food Programme, serving as Africa Policy Advisor from 1985 to 1989 and then as Area Director for Eastern Africa, contributing to famine-relief strategies and food security policies.

Haile Selassie's imperial parliament had two houses, the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, and it existed from 1931 to 1974. Under the 1931 constitution all members were appointed, primarily by the Emperor. The 1955 constitution reformed the Chamber of Deputies so that its members were to be elected.

During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, Italian troops seized Aksum on 15 October 1935. Its famous obelisk was torn from its site and sent to Rome to be placed in front of the Ministry of Colonies. Adwa had been conquered a few days earlier, on 6 October.

The Derg dissolved its military junta in 1987, becoming civilianized as the People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia under the Workers' Party of Ethiopia, in an attempt to maintain its rule. By then the country had been ravaged by the 1983-1985 famine, in which an estimated 400,000 to 590,000 people died, and by economic decline and the Derg's own policies, which increased popular support for the rebels. The Soviet Union began ending its support in the late 1980s, and the government was overwhelmed by increasingly victorious rebel groups.

In 1994, three years after the Derg regime fell, an Ethiopian court charged several former military officers with genocide and murder, saying it had documents showing a high-level order to assassinate Haile Selassie in 1975 for leading a "feudal regime". The court found them guilty of strangling the Emperor on his bed at the Jubilee Palace in Addis Ababa, on 27 August 1975. State media had reported that he died of "respiratory failure" after a prostate operation, a claim Asrat Woldeyes rejected. His bones, found in 1992 under a concrete slab on the palace grounds, were buried at the Holy Trinity Cathedral of Addis Ababa on 5 November 2000.

In 2009 the Parliament of Ethiopia passed Proclamation 654/2009, the Federal Flag Proclamation, which prohibited, among 23 other provisions, using the flag without its emblem or defacing it by writing or displaying signs, symbols, emblems or pictures. Most offenses were punishable by a fine of 3000 birr or rigorous imprisonment up to one year. The first offense, mandating use of the emblem, carried a heavier penalty of 5000 birr or rigorous imprisonment up to one year and six months. The 1996 Flag Proclamation it replaced had made no mention of offenses or penalties.

philosophy.text: Julius Nyerere's Ujamaa, meaning 'fraternity' in Swahili, was a socialist ideology behind Tanzania's development policies after independence from the United Kingdom in 1961. Within a year of independence, Nyerere introduced the Preventive Detention Act to crush opposition. From 1973 to 1975 the collectivizing goals were pursued through the forced villagization of Operation Vijiji, and according to Nyerere, over seven million people were moved between September 1973 and June 1975, and a further four million by the end of 1976. Peasants resisted leaving their individual farms, and Nyerere ordered forced movement to Ujamaa villages.

In late 2023, the publisher De Gruyter released the first English translation of the Hatata texts made outside Ethiopia. Titled The Hatata Inquiries, it presents two seventeenth-century African philosophical texts about reason, the Creator, and our ethical responsibilities.

Haile Selassie is accorded divine importance in Rastafari, an Abrahamic religion that emerged in the 1930s. Although Jamaican authorities expected him to reject the belief, he never rebuked the Rastafari for seeing him as God. Instead, he presented the movement's faithful elders with gold medallions.

In 1920, the Italian orientalist Carlo Conti Rossini claimed that the Hatata texts were really written by an Italian priest, Guisto de Urbino. This began a long scholarly dispute over whether the philosophy of Zera Yacob was authentically Ethiopian.

Between 1941 and 1959, Haile Selassie worked to make the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church self-governing. His appeals to the Coptic Church of Alexandria in 1942 and 1945 were denied. In 1959, Pope Kyrillos VI finally elevated the Abuna to Patriarch-Catholicos.

The Beta Israel first made extensive contact with other Jewish communities in the early 20th century, which sparked a rabbinic debate over whether they counted as Jewish. After halakhic and constitutional discussions, Israeli authorities decided in 1977 that they qualified under the Law of Return.

Nyerere argued that true liberation from colonialism required Tanzania to be economically self-sufficient. From 1968 to 1975 his government consolidated rural Tanzania into village-style farming communities where resources were shared collectively, in order to free Tanzanian culture from the capitalist values imposed under colonial rule. The program began as voluntary, but over time the state took control of village management and production in a way some historians have called coercive and autocratic. The forced collectivization of land that had once been family-owned was a sore point for many farmers, who bristled at the radical changes to their culture and lifestyle.

In 1934, the German scholar Eugen Mittwoch also argued that the philosophical Hatata texts could not have been written by an African. Sumner published a lengthy rebuttal of the claims of Rossini and Mittwoch in 1976. In 2017 he gained the support of the philologist Getatchew Haile.

Carlo Conti Rossini, who denied African authorship of the Hatata, published an article in September 1935 saying Abissinia was incapable of evolution and civil progress. Its argument was used to justify Italy's invasion of Ethiopia. After the conquest, he received a prize from the Mussolini regime in 1937.

Michael Manley visited Haile Selassie at his palace in Addis Ababa in October 1969, before becoming Jamaica's prime minister. The Emperor said he was confused by the Rastafarians' beliefs but respected them. He gave Manley the Rod of Correction, thought to have helped him win the 1972 election.

A Baháʼí from Alexandria, Egypt, Sabri Elais, introduced the Baháʼí Faith to Ethiopia in 1933, when he was 27 years old. This followed letters from `Abdu'l-Bahá in 1916 encouraging the religion to be taken to Africa. In November 1934 the first Baháʼí Local Spiritual Assembly in the country formed in Addis Ababa.
In 1919, Pope Benedict XV founded the Pontifical Ethiopian College within the Vatican walls. It used St. Stephen of the Abyssinians' Church, behind St. Peter's Basilica, as its designated church.

culture.text: Ethiopia's 2007 national census found that over 32 million people, or 43.5%, were Ethiopian Orthodox Christians. Over 25 million, or 33.9%, were Muslim, and 13.7 million, or 18.6%, were P'ent'ay Christians. Just under two million, or 2.6%, followed traditional beliefs.

From the 1950s to the 1970s, Ethiopian popular music flourished with performers such as Mahmoud Ahmed, Tilahun Gessesse and Alemayehu Eshete. Perhaps the most influential musician of the period was the Ethio-jazz innovator Mulatu Astatke.

Since their recognition under Israel's Law of Return, most of the Beta Israel, or Ethiopian Jews, have moved from Ethiopia to Israel through government initiatives starting in 1979. The journey meant crossing hazardous lowland regions and entailed significant hardship, and thousands perished, particularly during long waits in refugee camps in the Sudanese desert and in Addis Ababa. At the end of 2019, there were 155,300 Ethiopian Jews in Israel. About 87,500 of them were born in Ethiopia, and 67,800 were born in Israel to Ethiopian-born parents.

In the 2007 national census, over 32 million Ethiopians, or 43.5%, reported being Ethiopian Orthodox Christians. About 33.9% were Muslim and 18.6% were P'ent'ay Christians, while 2.6% followed traditional beliefs. Those who called themselves Hindu, Jewish, Baháʼí, agnostic or atheist were all counted as Other.

Ethiopia's government stated in 2016 that 67% of the country was Christian. It said 44% of the population belonged to the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. The Kingdom of Aksum had adopted Christianity as its state religion in the 4th century.

Several record labels shaped Ethiopian popular music in the 1950s to 1970s, including Amha Records, Kaifa Records and Philips-Ethiopia. Since 1997, Buda Musique's Éthiopiques series has compiled many of those singles and albums on compact disc.

Israeli authorities decided in 1977 that the Beta Israel qualified for the Law of Return. Operation Moses in 1984 and Operation Joshua in 1985 were part of Operation Brothers, which evacuated the community from Sudan between 1979 and 1990. Operation Solomon followed in 1991.

In May 2021, the exhibition The Wax and Gold of Hairstyles in Ethiopia opened at the Addis Ababa Museum. It showed photographs taken by German anthropologists in southern Ethiopia between 1934 and 1971, alongside modern drawings. In June 2022 it moved to Jinka for permanent display.

The Baháʼí Faith reached Ethiopia in 1933, when Sabri Elais, a 27-year-old Baháʼí from Alexandria, Egypt, introduced it. The first Baháʼí Local Spiritual Assembly in the country was formed in Addis Ababa in November 1934. Ethiopian Baháʼís elected a National Spiritual Assembly in 1962.

Ethiopia's Culture article notes that English is the most widely spoken foreign language and the medium of instruction in secondary schools. Amharic was once the language of primary school instruction but has been replaced in many areas by regional languages such as Oromiffa, Somali or Tigrinya. The 1995 Constitution gives all languages equal state recognition.

Between 2020 and 2023, Israel ran Operation Tzur Israel to bring thousands of Ethiopian community members, many with family in Israel, to the country. On July 15, 2023, 5000 Jews from Ethiopia reunited with family in Israel.

In November 2016, the two-year Creative Futures project, funded by the European Union, was launched in Ethiopia. Its partners were the British Council, Goethe-Institut and iceaddis, described as Ethiopia's first creative business hub. It aimed to invest in the creative economy and give young people job skills.
